article.scope_note: A heat-flow probe is an instrument system that measures temperature at depth in the regolith. The geothermal gradient multiplied by the thermal conductivity gives the heat flow from the interior, so the probe must measure temperature at several depths and needs a way to measure or estimate conductivity. This article covers the probe system. Single-point subsurface temperature sensors are payload 011 and stand-alone thermal conductivity probes are payload 010; they are referred to only where the heat-flow probe depends on them.
article.overview: The Moon loses heat from its interior. The rate of loss, the heat flow, depends on how hot the deep interior is and how it transports heat. Measuring it at the surface is one of the few direct ways to test models of the Moon's thermal history and its radioactive heat sources. In the sources read, Apollo was the only lunar mission to fly heat-flow probes. Two probes were installed by the Apollo 15 and Apollo 17 crews, after drilling holes in the regolith, and their data were used to estimate the heat flow at both sites [1][2]. The Apollo 16 instrument was damaged during installation and never operated, and the Apollo 13 hardware never reached the surface [1]. InSight's Heat Flow and Physical Properties Package (HP3) on Mars included a self-hammering probe, the mole, which failed to bury itself to its planned depth [4][5]. The 2020 NASA Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) study proposed two heat-flow probes on each lander, but these have not flown [8].
article.description: A heat-flow probe in the Apollo design had three parts. A thermometer string: twelve thermometers per probe, eight platinum resistance sensors in the lower part (about 1 m) and four thermocouples in the upper part (about 1.7 m) [2]. A borestem: two hollow fibreglass borestems, each 2.5 cm in outer diameter, designed to be inserted to 3 m and spaced 10 m apart [1]. An electronics and cable link: a surface electronics package, connected by a 9 m flat ribbon cable, sent the data to the ALSEP central station [1]. The HP3 mole was a different design: a self-hammering penetrator with a built-in heater and temperature sensors, connected to the lander by a tether carrying 14 platinum sensors [4][5]. The LGN probe was a pneumatic drill that inserts a boom carrying sensors [8].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of the probe is to measure heat flow from the interior. The measurement is made in four steps: measure temperature at several depths, derive the gradient, measure the thermal conductivity, then multiply the two. The Apollo experiment aimed to determine the lunar heat flux at its landing sites; the 1977 final report describes the results as a means to understand the Moon's internal thermal state [1]. The LGN study lists two science goals for a heat-flow measurement: determining the heat flux from the mantle, and measuring heat flux from the crust at different locations [8]. The LGN requirement is to determine heat flow to within 2 mW/m², with thermal conductivity and gradient each measured to 7% accuracy, at a minimum of three depths below 1.5 m [8]. The HP3 design aimed to measure heat flow on Mars to better than plus or minus 5 mW/m², and thermal conductivity to better than 3.5% (1 sigma) [4].
article.operating_principle: A heat-flow probe measures temperature at known depths. The gradient is the change in temperature with depth. A heater, or a deliberate thermal disturbance, is used to measure how quickly the material conducts heat [1][4]. Apollo: the probe's heaters were used to measure the regolith's thermal conductivity in place. In the short-term method, the heater warms the probe and the rate of cooling after the heater switches off gives the conductivity. In the long-term method, the team analysed the downward movement of annual and transient temperature waves, such as those produced by astronauts working nearby [1][2]. HP3: the mole is hammered into the regolith and measures conductivity with its heater; the design measured cooling after a heating phase, with a 24-hour conductivity measurement after each 50 cm advance [4]. LGN: the proposed probe measures gradient and conductivity at intervals as it is drilled, with a 2-hour thermal measurement at each depth [8].
article.scientific_importance: A heat-flow measurement is one of the few direct geophysical tests of the Moon's thermal evolution, because it measures how fast heat escapes from the interior. The Apollo results are, in the sources read, the only direct measurements of lunar heat flow [1][2]. The 2015 restoration paper notes that the Apollo heat-flow data are scientifically important but not fully archived. The processed record ends in December 1974, and the raw data from January 1975 to September 1977 were not archived [2].

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a heat-flow probe. The three examples below are different designs, one flown on the Moon, one flown on Mars and one proposed. They should not be compared directly.

examples.name: Apollo Heat Flow Experiment (Apollo 15 and 17)
examples.status: Flown on Apollo 15 and 17. The Apollo 16 instrument was installed but never operated after its cable was damaged. The Apollo 13 hardware never reached the surface [1][2].

probe_design.thermometer_layout: Eight platinum resistance sensors in the lower part (about 1 m; four per half-metre, with gradient and ring bridges) and four thermocouples in the upper part (about 1.7 m).
probe_design.sensor_type: Platinum resistance elements of 500 ohm for gradient sensors, each with a 1000-ohm heater wound on it.
probe_design.borestems: Two hollow fibreglass borestems, each 2.5 cm outer diameter, design depth 3 m, spaced 10 m apart.
probe_design.probe_length: The 1977 report gives 1.09 m when unfolded; the 2015 record gives an overall length of about 2.7 m. Not reconciled in the sources read.
probe_design.mass: Design limit about 4.5 kg per probe (1977 report); as-built mass not legible in the OCR text.
probe_design.power: Design peak 9 W (1977 report). Heater power values in the OCR text are unclear and are not used.
probe_design.stowage: Stowage compartment about 63 cm long; probes deeper than 60 cm had to be folded.
probe_design.data: A 7.25-minute measurement sequence; the surface electronics package sent data through the ALSEP central station.

deployment_outcomes.apollo_15: The drill stalled at about 1 m. The deepest sensor of probe 1 was at 137 cm. Holes recorded as 1 m and 1.5 m deep. The second probe was inserted, but its top protruded above the surface.
deployment_outcomes.apollo_16: The cable connecting the probe to the central station was caught and torn off cleanly at the connector during the first probe's insertion. NASA decided not to repair it; the instrument was not usable.
deployment_outcomes.apollo_17: Both borestems drilled to their prescribed depth, probes installed. Deepest sensor at 233 cm; holes recorded as 2.5 m deep.

observed_surface_heat_flow_mW_per_m2.source: 1977 final report, Table 1; consistent with the 2015 record [1][2].

heat_flow_results.best_estimate_apollo_15: 2.1 x 10^-6 W/cm2 (2.1 microW/cm2 = 21 mW/m2), uncertainty plus or minus 10%, mean of two probes, no terrain correction [1].
heat_flow_results.best_estimate_apollo_17: Observed mean 1.6 microW/cm2 (16 mW/m2), reduced to 1.4 microW/cm2 (14 mW/m2) after a minus 10% terrain correction [1].
heat_flow_results.conflict: A 1978 conference abstract (NTRS 19780005001) lists 3.1 and 2.2 microW/cm2 (31 and 22 mW/m2) with plus or minus 20% uncertainty. Those figures could not be traced to the primary report; this article uses the primary values [1][2][3].

thermal_conductivity.surface_layer: About 2 to 3 cm thick, density 1.1 to 1.2 g/cm3, conductivity 0.5 to 1.6 mW/(m K) [1].
thermal_conductivity.deeper_regolith: Density 1.75 to 2.10 g/cm3; conductivity about 10 to 15 mW/(m K). Averages below 10 cm: 10 mW/(m K) plus or minus 10% (Apollo 15), 15 mW/(m K) plus or minus 10% (Apollo 17) [1].
thermal_conductivity.methods: Short-term heater-activated tests in situ, and long-term analysis of the downward propagation of annual and transient temperature waves [1][2].

examples.monitoring_span: Apollo 15 probes July 1971 to January 1977; Apollo 17 probes December 1972 to September 1977 [2].

examples.name: InSight HP3 mole heat-flow probe (Mars)
examples.type: Flown Mars heat-flow probe (2018-2022); NOT a lunar system
examples.status: Flown on Mars. Included as a modern, flown heat-flow probe; no lunar operation is implied. The 2018 design paper gives pre-flight values [4]. The 2022 soil paper gives values from the flown mission but was read only partly, through a summary [5]. Labels: D (design), F (flown), P (planned).

mass_and_dimensions_D.science_tether: 75 g; 4855 mm long, 36 mm wide, 0.2 mm thick.
mass_and_dimensions_D.support_structure: 2085 g; 650 x 418 x 453 mm (excludes tether length monitor, mole and science tether).
mass_and_dimensions_D.back_end_electronics: 660 g; 200 x 84 x 150 mm; in the lander warm electronics box.
mass_and_dimensions_D.whole_package_mass_and_power_W: Not stated in the source read. The listed items sum to about 3.76 kg, excluding the radiometer.

examples.mole_design_D: Self-impelling, low-velocity penetrator. A tungsten hammer accelerated by a spring strikes an anvil on the hull; a drive mass 4.4 times the hammer mass re-tensions the spring. Hammering frequency 0.28 Hz. Each stroke advances 0.1 to 1 mm, depending strongly on regolith resistance. Planned penetration at least 3 m and up to 5 m. Planned cycle: about 50 cm advance, cooldown of at least 48 h, then a 24-hour conductivity measurement. Heater foils in the outer hull also serve as temperature sensors, commandable from 0 to 1 W each; number of foils not stated [4].
examples.temperature_sensors_D: 14 platinum resistance sensors (PT100) on the science tether, unequally spaced with more sensors near the mole. Accuracy for temperature differences 6.5 mK (1 sigma) [4].
examples.planned_accuracy_D_and_P: Heat flow better than plus or minus 5 mW/m2 (abstract); predicted heat-flow uncertainty 2.2 mW/m2 for nominal conditions (design table). Thermal conductivity better than 3.5% (1 sigma) [4].
examples.flown_outcome_F_from_partial_summary: Reached about 31 cm initially and a final tip depth of about 37 cm, with the back end 1 to 2 cm below the surface. Two reversal attempts extracted it by about 18 cm and about 5 cm. Reported failure mode: lack of friction in an unexpectedly thick cohesive duricrust; an external obstruction was ruled out after sol 311. Attempts stopped in early January 2021, about 22 months in, because power was needed for other instruments [5].
examples.soil_values_F_from_summary: Duricrust penetration resistance 0.3 to 0.7 MPa; layer below 30 cm 4.9 plus or minus 0.4 MPa; duricrust cohesion 2 to 15 kPa depending on friction angle. Values from a summary of the 2022 paper; check before use [5].
examples.data_path_D: Back-end electronics in the lander warm electronics box control all functions and store data in non-volatile memory, downlinked on lander wake-ups. Design data rates: 5.9 Mbit per sol for conductivity mode, 1.5 Mbit per sol for monitoring [4].

examples.name: Lunar Geophysical Network (LGN) heat-flow probes (proposed; not flown)
examples.status: Proposed. The 2020 LGN Decadal Study Final Report lists the mission as currently in formulation [8]. TRL about 5 for the Moon for the heat-flow probe [8]. The report names the probe LISTER and attributes the instrument to Texas Tech University and Honeybee Robotics [8]. The report states a CLPS flight in late 2022 or early 2023; this date has passed and the report cannot confirm it. Mission launch shown as 30 August 2030 [8]. No flight is confirmed in the sources read.
examples.number_and_deployment_proposed: Two probes per lander, deployed from two opposite legs, one at a time; a second probe is used if the first is blocked by a buried rock [8]. Pneumatic drill: a Kapton and glass-fibre composite boom driven down by gas jets at a penetrating cone, design depth 3 m. Drilling in 0.5 m steps with a 2-hour thermal measurement at each depth; 12 hours for the first probe's deployment to 3 m; probe 2 starts after probe 1 finishes monitoring and is shut down at night [8].
examples.mass_and_power_proposed: Heat-flow probe row of the study's instrument table: CBE mass 14.2 kg (18.5 kg with contingency); average CBE power 12.0 W (15.6 W with contingency). Not stated whether 14.2 kg is for the pair or each probe. Table alignment ambiguity recorded in payload 006; the CBE mass rows sum to 75.5 kg against a stated payload total of 76.5 kg [8].
examples.requirement_proposed: Heat flow within 2 mW/m2; thermal conductivity and gradient each to 7% accuracy; at least three depths below 1.5 m, spaced 0.3 m or more [8].
examples.risk_proposed: Buried large rocks could halt the drill. Mitigation: two probes per lander. Apollo sample analysis estimate: 0.2% probability of hitting a rock larger than 4 cm in 1 m of drilling [8].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Apollo probe: borestems 2.5 cm outer diameter, 3 m design depth; probe length 1.09 m unfolded (1977 report) or about 2.7 m overall (2015 record), not reconciled. HP3 mole: 27 mm by 400 mm; HP3 support structure 650 x 418 x 453 mm. LGN: dimensions not stated for the probe. These designs are not directly comparable.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Apollo: design limit about 4.5 kg per probe; as-built mass not legible. HP3: mole 860 g; whole-package mass not stated (listed items sum to about 3.76 kg excluding the radiometer). LGN: CBE 14.2 kg for the heat-flow probe row, per probe or pair not stated.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo: design peak 9 W. HP3: whole-package power in watts not stated (energy per mode in the design table is garbled). LGN: average CBE 12.0 W for the heat-flow probe row.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Thermal: the Apollo 16 instrument failed through mechanical damage to its cable during installation, not through a thermal event [1]. The HP3 design table gives component operating ranges, but row alignment in the extraction is uncertain, so these are not quoted [4]. The LGN probe operates at reduced cycles at night; probe-specific temperature range not stated [8]. Power: see physical_specifications.power_requirements. Data: Apollo probes sent data through the ALSEP central station [1]; HP3 stored data in the back-end electronics and downlinked on lander wake-ups [4]; LGN data rate 1.5 kbps [8]. Cable: the Apollo 16 failure shows that the flat cable is a single point of failure [1].
article.limitations: 1. Apollo probe lengths conflict: 1.09 m (1977 report, one probe assembly) vs about 2.7 m overall (2015 record). 2. Apollo 15 failure dates conflict: the 1977 report gives a first major failure in December 1975; the 2015 record states monitoring continued to January 1977. 3. Apollo heat-flow values: the primary 1977 report and the 2015 record both give 21 and 16 mW/m2; a 1978 abstract lists 3.1 and 2.2 microW/cm2 (31 and 22 mW/m2), not traceable to the primary report. 4. Apollo as-built mass and power are not legible in the OCR text. 5. Apollo raw data from January 1975 to September 1977 are not archived; only part has been recovered [2]. 6. HP3 flown values: the 2022 soil paper was read only through a summary; the whole-package mass and power are not stated. 7. LGN values are from a 2020 study, not a flight; per probe or per pair for 14.2 kg is not stated; the CLPS flight date has passed and is unverified. 8. Images: two verified; neither shows a lunar heat-flow probe. The Apollo 15 panorama shows deployment context only. 9. Scope: the probe system only, not single-point temperature sensors or stand-alone conductivity probes.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Apollo: probes stowed in a compartment about 63 cm long, folded when deeper than 60 cm; installed by the astronauts with the ALSEP lunar surface drill, one probe per hole; connected to the central station by a 9 m ribbon cable [1][2]. HP3 (Mars): back-end electronics in the lander warm electronics box; tether carries sensors to the mole [4]. LGN (proposed): pneumatic boom from a lander leg, one probe at a time; two probes per lander for redundancy [8]. No compatibility with any current or future lander is claimed for any heat-flow probe in this article.
transportation_process: Apollo: probes stowed in a compartment about 63 cm long; probes deeper than 60 cm folded [1].
Apollo: holes drilled with the ALSEP lunar surface drill; one probe installed per hole [1][2].
Apollo: each probe connected to the central station by a 9 m ribbon cable [1].
HP3 (Mars): back-end electronics in the lander warm electronics box; tether carries sensors to the mole [4]. The sources read do not describe how the mole was placed beyond the photograph.
LGN (proposed): probe deployed by a pneumatic boom from a lander leg, one at a time; two probes per lander for redundancy [8].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo: astronaut drilling and installation with the ALSEP drill [1][2]. LGN (proposed): pneumatic gas-jet drill with boom from a lander leg [8]. HP3: self-hammering mole, tethered to the lander [4][5].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15 and 17 Heat Flow Experiment (1971-1977) [1][2]; InSight HP3 on Mars (2018-2022) [4][5]; LGN proposal (2020 study) [8].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with any current or future lander is claimed for any heat-flow probe in this article.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo heat-flow experiment produced the only direct measurements of lunar heat flow in the sources read [1][2]. Successor concepts, including the LGN proposal, aim to measure heat flow at more locations, including the farside [8]. In the sources read, the HP3 mole is the only self-burying heat-flow probe flown. Its failure to reach its planned depth gives engineering lessons for future probes [4][5].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Apollo: the 1977 final report and the 2015 restoration record were read in full; the 1972 and 1974 Apollo chapters and the 1978 conference abstract were read as abstracts only [1][2][3][6][7]. HP3: the 2018 design paper was read in full [4]; the 2022 soil paper was read only partly, through a summary [5]. LGN: read from the local 2020 study copy [8]. Images: the HP3 mole and the Apollo 15 panorama were verified; no lunar heat-flow probe photograph was verified. Proposed claims: the LGN CLPS flight date and TRL have not been verified against a current source.

data_quality_notes: Scope: the heat-flow probe system only. Single-point subsurface temperature sensors (payload 011) and stand-alone thermal conductivity probes (payload 010) are excluded except where the probe depends on them.
Apollo probe length conflict: 1.09 m for one probe assembly (1977 report, p.259) vs about 2.7 m overall (2015 record). Not reconciled.

Apollo heat-flow values: the primary 1977 report (Table V-D-1, Table 1, p.124) and the 2015 record both give observed surface heat flow of 21 mW/m2 (Apollo 15) and 16 mW/m2 (Apollo 17). A 1978 abstract (NTRS 19780005001) gives 3.1 and 2.2 microW/cm2 with plus or minus 20%; not traceable to the primary report; not used for site values. A 1977 abstract (NTRS 19770051977) gives an average global heat flux of about 1.8 microW/cm2; a global estimate, not a site value; not used.
Apollo 15 failure date conflict: the 1977 report states a first major failure in December 1975; the 2015 record states Apollo 15 monitoring continued to January 1977. Not reconciled.

Apollo 15 probe depths: the 1977 report gives a deepest sensor at 137 cm and says probes were buried to shallower than planned depths; the 2015 record gives holes 1 m and 1.5 m deep. Compatible, not identical.
Apollo as-built probe mass, final cable mass and sample rate beyond the 7.25-minute cycle are not legible or not stated.
Apollo raw data from January 1975 to September 1977 are not archived; partial recovery from original ALSEP magnetic tapes is described in the 2015 record.
The Apollo 1972 and 1974 PSR chapters and the 1977 and 1978 conference abstracts were read as abstracts only; their internal design and correction details were not read.

HP3: the 2018 design paper was read in full; the 2022 soil paper was read only through a summary, and its numbers (duricrust penetration resistance, layer values, cohesion) must be checked against the PDF before publication.
HP3: whole-package mass and power in watts are not stated in the source read. The design table's energy-per-mode values and operating-temperature rows are garbled and were not quoted as definitive.
HP3: the number of heater foils and the planned stroke count are not stated.

LGN: the heat-flow probe row of Table 4 gives 14.2 kg CBE and 12 W CBE; whether these are for the pair or each probe is not stated. The mass rows sum to 75.5 kg against a stated payload total of 76.5 kg. The probe-specific operating temperature range is not stated.
LGN: the CLPS flight of the LISTER probe was stated for late 2022 or early 2023; that date has passed and the report cannot confirm a flight. Treated as proposed.
LGN: the local file's URL folder is dated 2024 while the report is dated 2020; the file-to-URL correspondence should be checked.

Images: two direct assets verified (PIA24263 Mars; Apollo 15 panorama). The Apollo 15 panorama shows deployment context; the probe and drill stem could not be identified in it. No lunar heat-flow probe photograph was verified.
No landing-site recommendations are included, in line with the user's deferral.
